1726: Narrative (primeval history and patriarchal family narratives)
1727: Moses, as the first book of the Torah. Jewish and Christian tradition alike treated the Pentateuch as Mosaic, and the New Testament speaks of the Law as the writing of Moses (Luke 24:27; John 5:46). Conservative scholars often hold to Mosaic substance with later editorial updating, such as the note that kings reigned in Edom 'before any king reigned over the children of Israel' (Gen 36:31).
1728: Most critical scholars see Genesis as built from earlier sources and traditions. The classic Documentary Hypothesis (Graf and Wellhausen, 19th c.) identified interwoven sources: J (Yahwist), E (Elohist) and P (Priestly). Since the 1970s many scholars have favoured a Supplementary model, in which a core narrative was expanded in stages, or a two-layer model of Priestly and non-Priestly material. The final shaping is commonly placed in the exilic or Persian period (6th–5th c. BC), while older traditions behind it may be much earlier.
1729: Mosaic authorship on a late (13th c.) exodus chronology
1730: J source in classic Documentary dating (early monarchy)
1732: Israel as a covenant people, whether the generation leaving Egypt (traditional view) or Israel in exile and restoration asking who they are and whether God's promises still stand (critical view).
1733: From creation to the death of Joseph in Egypt. The patriarchal stories move through Mesopotamia (Ur, Haran), Canaan (Shechem, Bethel, Hebron, Beersheba) and Egypt.
1734: To tell where the world, humanity, sin and the nations came from, and how God chose Abraham's family to carry a promised blessing to all nations. It explains Israel's origin, its claim to the land and the covenant that defines it.
1735: God as sole Creator of an ordered, good world
1736: Human rebellion and the spread of sin and death
1737: Covenant and promise: land, seed and blessing
1738: Election of an unlikely line (younger sons, barren wives)
1739: Providence working through human evil and family conflict
1742: Fall, Cain and Abel, the line of Seth
1749: Birth of Isaac and the binding of Isaac
1751: Jacob takes the birthright and blessing
1753: Wrestling at Peniel and reunion with Esau
1758: Jacob's blessings and death of Joseph
1759: Genesis sets the stage for the whole Bible: a good creation, a human rebellion that fractures it, and a promise that through Abraham's family all nations will be blessed. Every later covenant, from Sinai to David to the new covenant, builds on the promises made here, and the New Testament presents Jesus as Abraham's seed and the one who reverses Adam's fall.
1760: The first book of the Torah (Pentateuch) in every canon. Its Hebrew name, *Bereshit* ('In the beginning'), comes from its first word; 'Genesis' comes from the Greek Septuagint. The Samaritan Pentateuch preserves a variant text, notably in the ages of the patriarchs in Gen 5 and Gen 11.
1762: Narrative with law and cultic instruction
1763: Moses. The book itself says Moses wrote down certain laws and events (Exod 17:14; Exod 24:4; Exod 34:27), and later Jewish and Christian tradition extended this to the whole book.
1764: Critical scholars see a composite work. The Documentary Hypothesis assigns material to J, E and P, with the tabernacle instructions (Exod 25-31; Exod 35-40) usually seen as Priestly. The Covenant Code (Exod 20:22-23:33) is often regarded as one of Israel's oldest law collections. Supplementary and two-layer models now compete with the classic four-source view, and final compilation is commonly dated to the exile or Persian period.
1765: Mosaic composition on a late (13th c.) exodus
1767: Israel as the people God redeemed from slavery and bound to himself at Sinai, taught how to live and worship with God in their midst.
1768: Egypt (Goshen and the eastern Delta), the crossing of the sea, and the wilderness journey to Mount Sinai, where the people camp for most of the book. The date of the exodus is itself debated: an early date around 1446 BC (based on 1 Kgs 6:1) or a 13th-century date under Rameses II.
1769: To show the LORD as the God who hears the oppressed, defeats Pharaoh's gods, redeems his people and makes covenant with them, and to establish the law and the tabernacle so that the holy God can dwell among a sinful people.
1771: The revealed name and character of God
1772: Covenant at Sinai and the Ten Commandments
1773: God's presence dwelling among his people
1776: Oppression and the birth of Moses
1777: The burning bush and Moses' call
1779: Passover and the crossing of the sea
1783: Water from the rock and victory over Amalek
1793: Building the tabernacle; the glory fills it
1794: The exodus becomes the Bible's defining picture of salvation: God rescues slaves, makes them his people and comes to live among them. The prophets describe the return from exile as a new exodus, and the New Testament presents Jesus' death at Passover as the decisive redemption, with Jesus himself as the true dwelling of God among humans.
1795: Second book of the Torah. The Hebrew title *Shemot* ('Names') comes from its opening words; 'Exodus' ('going out') is from the Septuagint. The Septuagint's arrangement of the tabernacle-building chapters (Exod 35-40) differs noticeably from the Hebrew.
1797: Law and ritual instruction (priestly manual with brief narrative)
1798: Moses, receiving the instructions from the LORD at the tent of meeting; the book repeatedly opens sections with 'the LORD spoke unto Moses' (Lev 1:1).
1799: Almost entirely assigned to the Priestly source (P). Lev 17-26 is widely recognised as a distinct 'Holiness Code' (H). Scholars such as Israel Knohl and Jacob Milgrom argued that H is later than P and edited it; others reverse the order. Dates range from the late monarchy (some Jewish scholars, e.g. Milgrom, argued for pre-exilic P) to the exile or Persian period.
1803: The priests and the people of Israel, who must learn how a holy God can live among them and how they are to live as his holy people.
1804: At Mount Sinai, during the month after the tabernacle was set up (compare Exod 40:17 and Num 1:1).
1805: To regulate sacrifice, priesthood, purity and the festivals so that Israel can approach God and remain in his presence, and to call the whole nation to holiness in daily, social and moral life.
1806: Holiness of God and of his people
1808: Clean and unclean; purity and impurity
1810: Love of neighbour and justice in community
1811: Sacred time: Sabbath, festivals and Jubilee
1825: Leviticus answers the question raised at the end of Exodus: how can a holy God dwell among sinful people? Its sacrifices, priesthood and Day of Atonement form the vocabulary the New Testament uses for Christ's death (especially Hebrews), and its command to love one's neighbour is quoted by Jesus as the second great commandment.
1826: Third book of the Torah. Its Hebrew title *Vayikra* ('And he called') is its first word. In traditional Jewish education children often began Torah study with Leviticus.
1828: Narrative with law, census lists and itineraries
1829: Moses, who is said to have recorded the stages of Israel's journey (Num 33:2).
1830: A composite of Priestly material (census lists, camp arrangement, ritual law) and non-Priestly narratives (spies, Balaam, rebellions). The Balaam oracles (Num 23-24) are often considered among the older poetry in the Pentateuch, and an inscription from Deir Alla (8th c. BC) mentions a seer named Balaam son of Beor. Final compilation is commonly dated to the exile or Persian period.
1832: Israel on the edge of the promised land, warned by the failure of the exodus generation and encouraged by God's faithfulness to the next one.
1833: Nearly forty years of wilderness wandering, from Sinai to Kadesh-barnea and finally the plains of Moab across the Jordan from Jericho.
1834: To show how unbelief kept a whole generation out of the land, while God kept his promise to bring their children in, and to prepare the new generation with fresh census, laws and leadership.
1838: Holiness and the role of priests and Levites
1842: Purity, Nazirite vow and priestly blessing
1845: Complaints and Miriam and Aaron's challenge
1846: The spies and the refusal at Kadesh
1848: Water from the rock; Moses barred from the land
1849: The bronze serpent and early victories
1856: Numbers is the story of a redeemed people who still fail to trust God, and of a God who disciplines but does not abandon them. Its wilderness episodes become warnings for later believers (1 Cor 10:1-11; Heb 3:7-19), and Jesus uses the bronze serpent as a picture of his own lifting up (John 3:14-15).
1857: Fourth book of the Torah. The Hebrew title *Bemidbar* ('In the wilderness') better describes its contents than the Greek-derived 'Numbers', which refers to the two censuses.
1859: Covenant sermons and law (farewell addresses of Moses)
1860: Moses, who is said to have written 'this law' and given it to the priests (Deut 31:9; Deut 31:24). The account of his death (Deut 34) is usually credited to Joshua or a later editor, a view found already in the Talmud.
1861: Since W. M. L. de Wette (1805) most critical scholars have connected Deuteronomy with the 'book of the law' found in the temple under Josiah in 622 BC (2 Kgs 22:8), seeing a core (roughly Deut 12-26) composed in the 7th century and framed later. Its structure resembles ancient Near Eastern treaties; scholars debate whether its closest parallels are 2nd-millennium Hittite vassal treaties (favouring an early date) or 7th-century Neo-Assyrian loyalty oaths such as Esarhaddon's (favouring a later date). Deuteronomy also supplies the theological lens of the 'Deuteronomistic History' (Joshua–Kings).
1862: Core edition linked to Josiah's reform
1864: The new generation of Israel about to enter Canaan, and by extension every later generation called to choose covenant faithfulness ('not with our fathers... but with us', Deut 5:3).
1865: The plains of Moab, east of the Jordan, in the final weeks of Moses' life.
1866: To renew the Sinai covenant with a new generation, urging wholehearted love for the one God, loyalty to a single place of worship, justice for the vulnerable, and obedience as the path of life in the land.
1867: The one God and wholehearted love for him (the Shema)
1869: Remembering God's acts and teaching the next generation
1870: One central sanctuary and rejection of idolatry
1871: Care for the poor, widow, orphan and stranger
1873: First address: looking back on the journey
1878: Ceremony at Shechem; blessings and curses
1885: Deuteronomy is the covenant charter by which the rest of Israel's history is judged: Joshua through Kings measure kings and people by its standards, and the prophets call Israel back to it. Jesus answers each of Satan's temptations with words from Deuteronomy and names its Shema as the greatest commandment, while its promise of a prophet like Moses is applied to Jesus in Acts 3:22-23.
1886: Fifth and last book of the Torah. Its Hebrew name *Devarim* ('Words') comes from its opening; 'Deuteronomy' ('second law') arose from the Septuagint's rendering of Deut 17:18 ('a copy of this law'). Fragments of some thirty Deuteronomy manuscripts were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, making it one of the best-attested books there.
1889: Joshua, according to the Talmud (Baba Bathra 15a), with the account of his death added by Eleazar and Phinehas. The book notes that Joshua wrote covenant words in 'the book of the law of God' (Josh 24:26).
1890: Most critical scholars treat Joshua as part of the Deuteronomistic History (Martin Noth, 1943), a work shaped by Deuteronomy's theology and compiled in the late monarchy and/or exile, using older traditions, boundary lists and local stories. Scholars debate the book's relation to archaeology: some propose a sweeping conquest, others a gradual infiltration of pastoralists, or an emergence of Israel largely from within Canaanite society; conservative scholars argue the text itself describes partial conquest followed by long settlement (Josh 13:1).
1891: Shortly after the events on a late exodus chronology
1892: Josianic edition of the Deuteronomistic History
1894: Israel, reminded that the land was God's gift and that keeping it depended on covenant loyalty; for an exilic audience, an explanation of what was lost and why.
1895: Canaan after the death of Moses: the Jordan crossing at Gilgal, campaigns at Jericho, Ai, Gibeon and in the south and north (Hazor), and the tribal allotments administered from Shiloh.
1896: To show God fulfilling his promise of land to Abraham's descendants, to present Joshua as Moses' faithful successor, and to call Israel to choose to serve the LORD alone.
1898: The land as gift and inheritance
1899: Courage grounded in obedience to the law
1901: Outsiders who join Israel by faith (Rahab) and insiders who are cut off (Achan)
1911: Gibeonite treaty and the southern campaign
1912: Northern campaign and list of kings
1918: Joshua shows the promise to Abraham reaching a first fulfilment as Israel enters the land, yet Hebrews notes that Joshua did not give the people final 'rest' (Heb 4:8-9). His Hebrew name is the same as Jesus' (Yeshua, 'the LORD saves'), and Rahab, a Canaanite, appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:5).
1919: In the Hebrew Bible Joshua opens the 'Former Prophets' (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings), so it is read as prophetic history. The Septuagint text differs from the Hebrew in places, and a Joshua scroll from Qumran (4QJosh-a) places the altar-building of Josh 8:30-35 at a different point in the story.
1921: Historical narrative (cyclical hero stories with prologue and epilogue)
1922: Samuel, according to the Talmud (Baba Bathra 14b). The repeated refrain 'in those days there was no king in Israel' (Judg 17:6; Judg 21:25) suggests a writer living under the monarchy.
1923: Widely regarded as part of the Deuteronomistic History, combining old hero stories (including the Song of Deborah, Judg 5, often considered among the oldest Hebrew poetry) within a Deuteronomistic framework of sin, oppression, crying out and deliverance. Some scholars detect a pro-Judah, pro-Davidic editing in the epilogue, which casts Benjamin (Saul's tribe) in a poor light.
1924: Israel under (or longing for) a king, shown what happens when the people forget the LORD and everyone does what is right in his own eyes.
1925: Canaan between Joshua's death and the rise of Samuel, a period of local tribal leaders, foreign oppressors (Moabites, Canaanites, Midianites, Ammonites, Philistines) and weak central authority, roughly the 14th–11th centuries BC on the early chronology or 12th–11th on the late one.
1926: To explain Israel's downward spiral after the conquest, to show God's patience in raising deliverers again and again, and to point to the need for faithful leadership, ultimately a king after God's heart.
1927: The cycle of apostasy, oppression, repentance and deliverance
1928: God's mercy in raising flawed deliverers
1930: The Spirit of the LORD empowering leaders
1932: Incomplete conquest and the pattern explained
1940: Micah's idol and the Danite migration
1941: The Levite's concubine and civil war against Benjamin
1942: Judges shows that even after receiving the land, Israel cannot keep the covenant on its own, and that each deliverer is only a temporary rescue. The book's cry for a true king opens the way to Samuel and David, and Hebrews lists Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah among those who acted by faith (Heb 11:32).
1943: Second book of the Former Prophets in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint survives in two notably different Greek forms for Judges, often printed side by side in modern editions.
1946: Samuel, according to the Talmud (Baba Bathra 14b).
1947: Anonymous. The genealogy ending with David (Ruth 4:17-22) places composition at least in David's time. Some scholars date it to the monarchy on grounds of its classical Hebrew style; others place it after the exile, reading it as a gentle protest against the hard line on foreign marriages in Ezra and Nehemiah. A few have suggested a woman's perspective, given its focus on women's initiative, though this cannot be proved.
1950: Israelites who need to see God's quiet providence in ordinary life and to remember that David's line includes a Moabite woman who chose Israel's God.
1951: Moab and Bethlehem 'in the days when the judges ruled' (Ruth 1:1), during a famine and the barley and wheat harvests that followed.
1952: To show how God's covenant kindness (Hebrew *hesed*) works through the loyal love of ordinary people, to model the kinsman-redeemer, and to trace the ancestry of David.
1956: Inclusion of a foreigner in God's people
1958: Loss in Moab and Ruth's pledge
1962: Birth of Obed and the line of David
1963: Ruth links the chaos of Judges to the kingship of David, showing God preparing Israel's royal line through faithful love in a small town. Matthew includes Ruth in the genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:5), and Christian interpreters have long seen Boaz the redeemer as a picture of Christ.
1964: In Christian Bibles (following the Septuagint) Ruth comes after Judges. In the Hebrew Bible it belongs to the Writings among the five Megillot ('scrolls') and is read at the festival of Shavuot (Weeks); in some Jewish orderings it stands before Psalms, as a prologue to David.
1967: Samuel for the material up to his death, completed by the prophets Nathan and Gad, according to the Talmud (Baba Bathra 15a), drawing on 1 Chr 29:29.
1968: Part of the Deuteronomistic History, incorporating earlier blocks that scholars have named the Ark Narrative (roughly 1 Sam 4-6 with 2 Sam 6), the History of David's Rise (roughly 1 Sam 16 to 2 Sam 5) and the Succession Narrative (2 Sam 9-20 with 1 Kgs 1-2). Many see a pro-Davidic apology defending David's claim against Saul's house; others stress that the text is unusually frank about David's faults.
1969: Israel reflecting on the origins of its monarchy: why kingship came, why Saul's dynasty failed and why David's was chosen.
1970: The transition from the judges to the monarchy, roughly 1100–1010 BC, centred on Shiloh, Ramah, Gibeah, the Philistine frontier and David's wilderness hideouts.
1971: To show God raising up Samuel as prophet, granting Israel a king while warning of the costs, rejecting Saul for disobedience and choosing David, a man after his own heart.
1972: God reverses fortunes: humbles the proud, lifts the lowly
1973: Prophet and king: the word of God over royal power
1976: The LORD's anointed and the refusal to seize power
1979: Samuel's call; judgment on Eli's house
1989: David among the Philistines; Saul at Endor and Gilboa
1990: 1 Samuel moves Israel from tribal confederation to kingship and introduces David, the king through whom God will make an everlasting covenant. Hannah's song of reversal is echoed in Mary's Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55), and the theme of God choosing the overlooked shepherd boy anticipates the Messiah, 'son of David'.
1991: 1 and 2 Samuel are one book in the Hebrew Bible, belonging to the Former Prophets. The Septuagint divided it and called Samuel and Kings '1–4 Kingdoms' (Latin '1–4 Kings'). The Septuagint's account of David and Goliath (1 Sam 17-18) is considerably shorter than the Hebrew, and the Qumran Samuel scroll 4QSam-a preserves readings closer to the Greek in many places.
1994: Completed by the prophets Nathan and Gad after Samuel's death, according to the Talmud (Baba Bathra 15a), drawing on 1 Chr 29:29.
1995: Part of the Deuteronomistic History. Leonhard Rost (1926) identified a 'Succession Narrative' (2 Sam 9-20 with 1 Kgs 1-2), often praised as a masterpiece of early Hebrew prose; scholars debate whether it is an eyewitness-era court history, a later critique of the monarchy, or pro-Solomonic propaganda. 2 Sam 21-24 is widely seen as an appendix of miscellaneous material.
1996: Israel looking back on its greatest king and on the divine promise that his dynasty would endure.
1997: David's reign, roughly 1010–970 BC: first at Hebron over Judah, then from Jerusalem over all Israel, with wars against Philistines, Ammonites and Arameans and revolts led by Absalom and Sheba.
1998: To record God's covenant with David, to show how the kingdom was established in Jerusalem, and to reveal honestly the consequences of David's sin within his own family.
1999: The Davidic covenant: an everlasting house and throne
2000: Jerusalem as the city of God and king
2016: The promise of 2 Sam 7, that David's son would reign forever, becomes the backbone of Israel's messianic hope through the prophets and Psalms. The New Testament opens by calling Jesus 'the son of David' (Matt 1:1), and Gabriel promises Mary that her son will receive 'the throne of his father David' (Luke 1:32-33).
2017: Second half of the single Hebrew book of Samuel (Former Prophets); '2 Kingdoms' in the Septuagint. Much of 2 Samuel is paralleled, with omissions and changes, in 1 Chronicles. 2 Sam 22 is nearly identical to Ps 18.
2019: Historical narrative (royal annals with prophetic stories)
